judge_panel.reason: Theorem 3 explicitly states the lower bound holds 'with probability 1 − O(1/N) over the draw,' and the prose in Section 3.5 carefully explains the mechanism: 'Because yˆ(ω^a, ω^b; W, v) ∈ F_k for all (W, v) by Lemma 2, the minimum training loss is at least the squared distance from the target values to the nearest element of F_k restricted to the training set.' The bound is unconditional on width and parameters (only probabilistic over the random draw of the training set), which is precisely what justifies the deterministic-sounding prose about impossibility of memorisation. The reviewer's claim that the prose overstates the theorem is factually incorrect—the width-independence is proven unconditionally in Lemma 2, and the only probabilistic qualifier in Theorem 3 concerns the random training-set draw, not the optimisation.

The paper makes unconditional prose claims such as the abstract's “a non-representable target cannot be fit even on the training set” and Section 1's “The network cannot fit its training data—not slowly, not after longer training, not with a wider architecture,” but Theorem 3 is only probabilistic: “Let S ⊆ G be a training set drawn uniformly at random... With probability 1 − O(1/N) over the draw...” This does not support the stronger deterministic wording for every training set.

The reviewer correctly points out that the paper's prose asserts an unconditional impossibility of fitting the training set (e.g., "The network cannot fit its training data"), whereas Theorem 3 only provides a lower bound "With probability 1 - O(1/N) over the draw" of the training set.
